title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 213: Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: Geothermal Energy
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 213 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: The Geothermal Frontier

Paragraph 1. Deep beneath Iceland's volcanic landscape lies an enormous source of clean power. While most nations burn fossil fuels or rely on changeable wind and sunshine, Iceland produces nearly one hundred percent of its electricity and home heat from domestic renewables, mainly geothermal energy. Located across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge—where two giant tectonic plates slowly pull apart—Iceland sits directly above rising underground magma, turning a once coal-dependent island into an energy pioneer.

Paragraph 2. Conventional geothermal power relies on natural underground water cycles. Rainwater seeps through porous volcanic cracks deep into the crust near hot magma chambers. Although temperatures reach several hundred degrees, intense underground pressure keeps the water from boiling. When engineers drill production wells one to three kilometres down, the sudden drop in pressure turns the superheated liquid violently into high-pressure steam, which rises up steel pipes to spin electricity turbines.

Paragraph 3. In the capital Reykjavik, geothermal water completely transformed urban life. In the early 1900s, the city choked under thick smoke from burning soft coal to warm wooden homes. Starting in 1930, city officials built insulated underground pipes delivering natural hot water straight into house radiators, heating over ninety-nine percent of greater Reykjavik today. Surplus warm water even flows through coiled plastic tubes beneath pavements and sidewalks, automatically melting winter snow without harmful de-icing salts.

Paragraph 4. Even clean geothermal extraction brings gas challenges. Deep reservoir water carries dissolved carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, which smells like rotten eggs and irritates lungs. To solve this, the Carbfix project at Hellisheidi plant captures waste gases, mixes them into water, and pumps the fluid into porous basalt rock, turning gas permanently into solid white stone within two years.

Paragraph 5. Looking ahead, the Iceland Deep Drilling Project (IDDP) is testing even deeper limits. Instead of standard wells reaching one to three kilometres, IDDP drills nearly five kilometres deep into 'supercritical' zones hotter than 450°C. Fluid here carries up to ten times more energy than standard steam, meaning one deep well could match ten normal wells while using far less surface land.

groups.title: Questions 8–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

q1.text: What geological feature explains Iceland's abundant geothermal energy?
options: A. Deep glacial lakes formed during recent ice ages
B. Heavy seasonal monsoons along coastal mountains
C. Two tectonic plates separating and bringing magma near the surface
D. Huge underground deposits of ancient black coal

steps: Đoạn 1: Nằm trên sống núi giữa Đại Tây Dương nơi hai mảng kiến tạo tách rời, magma dâng gần mặt đất.

q2.text: Why doesn't deep underground water boil before engineers drill into it?
options: A. Intense underground pressure stops the water from boiling.
B. Cold rainwater cools down the magma chambers.
C. Porous volcanic cracks absorb all the heat instantly.
D. Thick basalt walls keep the water temperature below 100°C.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...intense underground pressure keeps the water from boiling."

q3.text: What extra winter benefit does Reykjavik's excess hot water provide?
options: A. It keeps outdoor swimming pools frozen for skating.
B. It filters polluted rainwater before it enters rivers.
C. It warms outdoor greenhouses to export tropical fruit.
D. It melts snow on walkways without needing chemical salts.

steps: Đoạn 3: Làm tan tuyết trên vỉa hè tự động mà không cần muối hóa chất.

q4.text: Why are researchers excited about the IDDP deep-drilling project?
options: A. It eliminates the need for any steel pipes or turbines.
B. One ultra-deep well could match ten normal wells using less land.
C. It operates entirely without rainwater seeping underground.
D. It allows factories to burn soft coal safely indoors.

steps: Đoạn 5: Một giếng siêu sâu có thể bằng 10 giếng thường và tốn ít diện tích đất bề mặt hơn.
Đoạn 2: "...turns the superheated liquid violently into high-pressure steam..."
Đoạn 4: "...turning gas permanently into solid white stone..."

q8.text: Before 1930, Reykjavik experienced heavy air pollution from burning soft coal.

steps: Đoạn 3: "In the early 1900s, the city choked under thick smoke from burning soft coal..."

q9.text: Most European countries have already copied Iceland's Carbfix stone-storage method.

steps: Đoạn 4: Chỉ mô tả dự án Carbfix tại nhà máy Hellisheidi ở Iceland, không nói các nước châu Âu khác đã sao chép.

q10.text: The IDDP boreholes are shallower than standard geothermal wells.

steps: Đoạn 5: Giếng thường sâu 1–3 km, còn giếng IDDP sâu gần 5 km (sâu hơn chứ không nông hơn).
